title: Electrical materials
description: Connect current and resistance to the band structure that makes a material a conductor, semiconductor or insulator.

sections.title: Relate voltage, current and resistance
sections.body: For an ohmic conductor at fixed physical conditions, Ohm's law is V = IR. Voltage V is measured in volts, current I in amperes and resistance R in ohms. A specimen's resistance depends on its material and geometry. Resistivity ρ is a material property in the stated conditions; for a uniform specimen, R = ρL/A, where L is length and A is cross-sectional area.

sections.title: Two equations to keep distinct
sections.body: Ohm's law: V = IR. Geometry and material: R = ρL/A. Therefore ρ = RA/L. Use consistent units; for SI, ρ is in Ω·m when R is in Ω, L in m and A in m².

sections.title: Worked example · calculate resistance and resistivity
sections.body: A wire carries 0.50 A when 6.0 V is applied. Its resistance is R = V/I = 6.0/0.50 = 12 Ω. If the wire is 2.0 m long with cross-sectional area 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m², then ρ = RA/L = (12)(1.0 × 10⁻⁶)/2.0 = 6.0 × 10⁻⁶ Ω·m. This illustrative calculation applies the equations; it is not a measurement reported in the lecture.

sections.title: Check assumptions and units
sections.body: V = IR is not a universal straight-line law for every material or every condition; the lecture notes that it applies to most, not all, materials. Do not confuse resistance, which depends on specimen dimensions, with resistivity, which characterizes the material under stated conditions.

sections.title: 30-second recap
sections.body: Use V = IR for an ohmic specimen. Use R = ρL/A to account for dimensions; longer means more resistance, larger area means less.

sections.title: From atomic levels to solid bands
sections.body: When many atoms form a solid, interactions split and broaden their allowed electron energy levels into bands. The valence band contains bound valence electrons; the conduction band contains states in which electrons can move through the solid. The forbidden gap separates allowed bands. Its size and occupancy help explain electrical behaviour.

sections.title: Compare the band pictures
items: Conductors: valence and conduction bands overlap or the conduction band is partly occupied, so mobile carriers are available.
Semiconductors: a relatively small band gap allows some carriers to reach the conduction band; conductivity changes with conditions.
Insulators: a large gap leaves very few carriers in the conduction band under ordinary conditions.
These are useful band-model descriptions; real conductivity also depends on temperature, impurities and material structure.

sections.title: Worked example · predict a category
sections.body: A material whose valence and conduction bands overlap has accessible mobile electrons without first crossing a substantial forbidden gap. The band model therefore predicts conductor-like behaviour. If instead the gap is small, a modest thermal or optical input can create carriers and the material may behave as a semiconductor. A large gap makes carrier creation much harder, which is the insulator picture.

sections.title: Do not call the bands physical layers
sections.body: Valence and conduction bands are allowed electron-energy ranges, not layers inside the material. Band diagrams explain available states; they do not mean electrons literally move through a physical gap.

sections.title: 30-second recap
sections.body: Band overlap gives conductors many available carriers; a small gap characterizes semiconductors; a large gap makes an insulator difficult to conduct.

sections.title: Low resistivity is useful in conductors
sections.body: Electrical conductors are selected to carry current with low resistive loss. The lecture focuses on conducting materials used in electrical machines and equipment. Copper is highlighted for high conductivity and useful fabrication properties; aluminium is lightweight and used in conductors, including aluminium-conductor steel-reinforced (ACSR) construction.

sections.title: Material choice is a trade-off
items: Copper: high conductivity and useful malleability, weldability and solderability; purity affects conductivity.
Aluminium: lower mass than copper and used in overhead conductors; ACSR adds a central steel core for mechanical support.
Impurities and alloying can increase resistivity, so conductivity alone does not determine the best engineering choice.

sections.title: Worked example · choose a transmission wire
sections.body: For a long overhead line, low mass and mechanical strength matter alongside electrical resistance. Aluminium is lighter, and an ACSR design combines aluminium conducting strands with a steel reinforcing core. For compact equipment windings where conductivity and fabrication are priorities, copper may be preferred. The choice depends on the design constraints rather than a single “best metal.”

sections.title: Keep conductivity and strength separate
sections.body: A mechanical support core is not the main current-carrying material just because it is part of the conductor assembly. Also avoid claiming that aluminium is always superior to copper; weight, size, mechanical requirements and connections matter.

sections.title: 30-second recap
sections.body: Copper offers high conductivity; aluminium offers low mass and is used in ACSR. Select for the whole application, not conductivity alone.

sections.title: A small band gap makes control possible
sections.body: Semiconductors have electrical conductivity between typical conductors and insulators, and their conductivity can be controlled. The lecture identifies silicon and germanium as elemental semiconductors with a small band gap. In a pure (intrinsic) semiconductor, thermal energy can create an electron and a hole; both carrier types are present.

sections.title: Doping adds a controlled impurity
items: Intrinsic: chemically pure semiconductor; electrons and holes are generated in pairs.
n-type: dope silicon with a pentavalent atom such as phosphorus; the extra valence electron can become mobile, so electrons are majority carriers.
p-type: dope silicon with a trivalent atom such as boron; an incomplete bond creates a hole, so holes are majority carriers.
Doping changes carrier concentration and conductivity; it does not turn the whole crystal into a charged object.

sections.title: Worked example · classify the dopant
sections.body: Add a small amount of phosphorus (five valence electrons) to silicon, whose atoms form four covalent bonds. Four phosphorus electrons can participate in bonding, leaving an extra electron that can move: the doped crystal is n-type. Add boron (three valence electrons) instead and one bond has an electron deficiency, creating a hole: the crystal is p-type.

sections.title: Temperature also changes conductivity
sections.body: The lecture notes that at 0 K carriers are frozen in the valence band and a semiconductor behaves as an insulator. As temperature rises, more carriers can be excited and semiconductor conductivity increases (resistivity decreases). This temperature trend is opposite to the common behaviour of metallic conductors.

sections.title: Do not swap majority carriers
sections.body: n-type means electrons are the majority carriers, not that the crystal has a net negative charge. p-type means holes are the majority carriers, not that the crystal is a net positive ion.

sections.title: 30-second recap
sections.body: Pure silicon is intrinsic. Phosphorus donor → n-type/electron majority; boron acceptor → p-type/hole majority. Semiconductor conductivity generally rises with temperature.

sections.title: Insulators resist ordinary current flow
sections.body: An insulator has a large forbidden energy gap, so ordinary conditions leave very few mobile carriers in its conduction band. The lecture gives a gap of about 15 eV as a simplified illustration and lists glass, insulating resins, laminates and enamels as examples used in electrical applications.

sections.title: Zero resistance below a critical temperature
sections.body: A superconductor is a material that enters a superconducting state below a material-dependent critical (transition) temperature, with zero electrical resistance. The lecture also describes magnetic-field expulsion, the Meissner effect. Its example is mercury, which becomes superconducting near 4 K.

sections.title: Worked example · insulation or superconductivity?
sections.body: A glass spacer in an electrical assembly is chosen to resist current at ordinary operating conditions: that is an insulating role. A mercury sample cooled below its critical temperature is instead a superconductor; it does not merely become a better ordinary conductor, but enters a distinct state with zero resistance and the Meissner effect.

sections.title: Temperature is part of the definition
sections.body: Do not call a material superconducting at every temperature. It must be below its critical temperature and in the superconducting state. Zero resistance and the Meissner effect are the key distinctions in this lecture.

sections.title: 30-second recap
sections.body: Large band gap → few carriers and insulating behaviour. Below its critical temperature, a superconductor has zero resistance and expels magnetic field.

questions.prompt: A 12 Ω resistor carries 0.50 A. What voltage is across it?
For a uniform wire, which change reduces resistance if material and length stay fixed?
options: Replace metres with centimetres without conversion
questions.explanation: R = ρL/A, so increasing area decreases resistance.

questions.prompt: What is the key band-model feature of a conductor?
options: Overlapping or partly occupied bands that provide mobile carriers
questions.explanation: Band overlap or partial occupation makes mobile carriers readily available.

questions.prompt: Why can a semiconductor conduct more as its temperature rises?
options: Its band gap disappears in every case
More charge carriers can be thermally excited
It becomes a metal with no temperature dependence
questions.explanation: Thermal energy can excite more carriers across the small gap, increasing conductivity.

questions.prompt: Which application detail best matches the lecture's copper discussion?
options: High conductivity and useful fabrication properties
Used only as an electrical insulator
Its conductivity is unaffected by impurities
It is the steel core in ACSR
questions.explanation: The lecture highlights copper's conductivity, malleability, weldability and solderability.

options: A copper core with a plastic outer shell
A steel support core with surrounding aluminium wires
questions.explanation: ACSR uses a central steel core surrounded by aluminium conductor strands.

questions.prompt: Phosphorus-doped silicon is usually classified as:
options: p-type, with holes as majority carriers
n-type, with electrons as majority carriers
questions.explanation: Pentavalent phosphorus contributes an extra mobile electron, making silicon n-type.

questions.prompt: What carrier is associated with boron-doped p-type silicon?
questions.explanation: Trivalent boron leaves an electron deficiency in the bonding structure, represented as a hole.

questions.prompt: Which statement about p-type material is correct?
options: The whole crystal has net positive charge
Holes are majority carriers, but the crystal remains electrically neutral overall
It must be doped with phosphorus
questions.explanation: p-type names its majority carrier; the doped crystal is not a macroscopic positive ion.

questions.prompt: What is the role of a large forbidden gap in an insulator?
options: It makes mobile carriers difficult to create under ordinary conditions
It guarantees zero resistance at room temperature
It makes valence and conduction bands overlap
It causes all electrons to leave the material
questions.explanation: A large gap leaves few electrons in the conduction band under ordinary conditions.

questions.prompt: Below what condition does a material enter its superconducting state?
questions.explanation: The critical temperature marks the transition into the superconducting state.

questions.prompt: Which phenomenon is the expulsion of magnetic field from a superconducting state?
questions.explanation: The lecture identifies magnetic-field expulsion as the Meissner effect.
